title: Who gets the last packets?
hook: There are 340 packets of Maggi and 200,000 people adding them to cart. Where does the system make the stock promise?
context: Flash sale checkout with a single limited SKU
solution_brief: Cart shows an estimate, not a promise. At Place order, atomically reserve one unit with a short expiry. The checkout path owns the critical counter; expired reservations return stock, and confirmed payment commits the order idempotently.

steps.prompt: 340 packets of Maggi are left and 200,000 people are adding them to their carts. What should Add to cart mean for stock?

options.text: Intent only: the cart shows availability but holds no stock.
A 30-minute reservation, so nobody loses the item they have just chosen.
A reservation that lasts until the shopper closes the browser.

steps.explanation: A cart records intent, and if every Add to cart held a unit, the first 340 clicks would lock up the whole stock in carts that mostly never become orders. A timed reservation at this stage has the same problem, only for 30 minutes at a time. A reservation tied to the browser session can strand units for as long as a tab stays open.
steps.bottleneck_note: A cart is intent; it is not yet a stock guarantee.
steps.context_note: Add to cart is the first click, long before anyone has paid.

steps.prompt: Two buyers press Place order at the same moment for the one remaining packet. How should the system pick exactly one winner?

options.text: One conditional atomic decrement that succeeds only while stock is at least 1.
Read the stock, check it is above zero in the application, then write stock minus one.
Process orders in the order of the click times that their browsers report.

steps.explanation: Making the check and the decrement one indivisible step means the database lets exactly one order through and rejects the other. Reading and then writing leaves a window in which both requests see a stock of one. Browser clocks differ and can be wrong, so they cannot order requests fairly or safely.
steps.bottleneck_note: The invariant is reserved plus sold never exceeds 340.
steps.context_note: Only one unreserved packet remains, and two orders arrive together.

steps.prompt: A buyer reserved one packet at checkout but never paid. What stops that packet from staying trapped?

options.text: A short expiry that returns the unit to stock, safe to apply twice.
A reminder email asking the buyer to pay or cancel.
A nightly job that releases every reservation older than 24 hours.

steps.explanation: A timeout frees the unit even when the browser never returns, and making the release idempotent means a retry or a race with a late payment cannot double-count it. A reminder email relies on the buyer acting, and a nightly sweep leaves scarce stock frozen for hours while other buyers see sold out.
steps.bottleneck_note: Expiry recovery must work even if the browser never returns.
steps.context_note: Each reserved packet is now held for a buyer, and some buyers will walk away in the middle of payment.

steps.prompt: A shopper's cart page says 12 left, but the authoritative stock counter says 0. What should checkout do when they press Place order?

options.text: Refuse the reservation on the real counter and say the estimate changed.
Accept the order, because the shopper saw 12 and was effectively promised stock.
Accept the order and cancel the surplus orders after the sale ends.
Trust the cache if it was refreshed within the last 10 seconds.

steps.explanation: The authoritative counter is the only thing that can promise a unit, so checkout must follow it even when the page said otherwise. Accepting orders against a stale view means overselling, and cancelling later turns a refusal into a broken promise. A fresher cache is still only an estimate.
steps.bottleneck_note: Cached availability can guide display, never authorize the last unit.
steps.context_note: The cart page reads a cached availability value that can lag behind the real counter.

steps.prompt: As stock nears zero, cart pages are getting far more traffic than checkout. How should the cart page present availability?

options.text: As an estimate, with the promise made only when checkout reserves a unit.
As 'In stock' until the counter reaches zero, since that is what the data says.
As an exact figure read from the stock counter on every cart view.

steps.explanation: Honest, softer wording keeps expectations right, and the hot counter stays reserved for the few shoppers who actually check out. A confident 'In stock' promises something the cart cannot deliver. Reading the real counter on every view puts 200,000 shoppers on the one resource that is already contended.
steps.bottleneck_note: Only checkout needs to contend on the critical counter.
steps.context_note: Cart views now outnumber checkout attempts by a huge margin, and none of them hold stock.
